opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a mix of curiosity and necessity. Back then, deep learning wasn't the mainstream thing it is today. Neural networks were still a bit of a niche topic, and when I started working on my undergraduate project, I quickly realized that training these models on a CPU was painfully slow. You'd wait a very long time just to see whether an idea worked.

Around the same time, people were starting to talk about using GPUs for general-purpose computing. CUDA had come out, and there was this sense that graphics cards, which were built for games, could actually do a lot of parallel number crunching. Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplications and similar operations, so the fit seemed natural. I thought, why not try it?

So I just dove in. There weren't many libraries to rely on, so I ended up writing a lot of the kernels myself and learning how the hardware actually worked: memory hierarchy, how threads were organized, all of that. It was frustrating at times, because when things broke you didn't get much help, but it was also very rewarding. When I saw the speedup, it felt a bit magical.

Looking back, that experience shaped a lot of what I did later. It taught me that the bottleneck in machine learning often isn't just the algorithm. It's also the system underneath it. If you can make experiments faster and easier to run, you change what people are able to explore. That idea stayed with me through things like XGBoost and later TVM and machine learning compilation. In a way, that small graduation project was where I first got hooked on the intersection of machine learning and systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate says CPU training was painfully slow, but does not identify FFT-optimized convolutional networks or MATLAB as the source of the persistent slowness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came out of necessity more than any grand vision. This was around 2010, when I was an undergraduate at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and I'd gotten interested in deep learning after reading some of the early papers on restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks. For my graduation project I wanted to train these models on something reasonably sized, and I very quickly ran into the wall everyone hits: a CPU just wasn't fast enough. I'd set up an experiment, go to sleep, and it still wouldn't be done in the morning.

Around that time I'd seen a few mentions that people were starting to use graphics cards for general-purpose computation, and the matrix operations at the heart of these models are exactly the kind of thing GPUs are good at. So I thought, why not try it. I got hold of a card, started learning CUDA, and the first results were really striking. Things that took hours suddenly took minutes. That experience shaped a lot of what I did later. It taught me that the choice of system and hardware isn't a side detail in machine learning. It really decides what experiments you can even attempt, and that line of thinking eventually led me toward building systems like XGBoost, MXNet, and TVM.

r001.rationale: The candidate says CPU training of restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks was too slow, prompting CUDA use. It does not identify FFT-optimized convolutional networks in MATLAB as the persistent performance problem.

I wanted to try ideas and get results faster, so I started looking at GPUs. CUDA gave me a way to explore that directly—to think about how the computation could run in parallel and then implement it myself. The motivation was really to make the experiments run faster, and that got me interested in the systems side of machine learning.

So the motivation was quite practical: I had a problem I wanted to solve, and learning CUDA became part of solving it.
